title: Maximus of Tyre: statues of words, men, beasts, gold and ivory help reach a God beyond sense
source_text: XXI. Quibus consona leguntur apud Maximum Tyrium, oratione qua disquirit, Utrum statuae sint ponendae Diis? Ubi postquam praestituit Deum esse omnium quae sunt Patrem ac conditorem, sole antiquiorem, antiquiorem coelo, tempore & aevo majorem, subjungit, Cum vero ejus essentia nostros sensus excedat, petimus subsidium a verbis, ab hominibus, & animalibus, ab auri eboris argentique figuris, &c. ut per haec ad intelligentiam numinis pertingamus.
pass_a_gloss: Things consonant with these are read in Maximus of Tyre, in the oration in which he inquires, Whether statues are to be set for the Gods? Where after he has laid down that God is the Father and founder of all things that are, older than the sun, older than heaven, greater than time and age, he subjoins, But when his essence exceeds our senses, we seek aid from words, from men, and animals, from figures of gold, ivory, and silver, &c., that through these we may arrive at the understanding of the divinity.
pass_b_english: Maximus asks whether gods should have statues, then answers with a ladder of aids—words, men, beasts, precious figures—toward a God beyond sense.
